latin.236:
§. VIII.
Utriusque, dicti Moliminis, Lipsiaci & Cassellani fructus haud exiguus fuit, qui se non ad suum tantùm, in quo suscepta sunt, paucisque abhinc annis finitum, sed modernum etiam non ita diu coeptum Seculum extendit.
latin.237: Nam praeterquàm quòd meliores utriusque Partis Theologi, mitius dehinc benigniusque de se mutuo Sectisque suis, sentire assuevêre, auditoresque suos ad idem faciendum, exemplis suis induxêre; ita Magistratus suos amore ac desiderio Pacis Ecclesiasticae conciliandae magis magisque implevêre.
latin.238: Post Lipsiacum enim Colloquium, Carolus Ludovicus Palatinus pacificum Institutum prae manibus habuit, Autori nostro celebratum, licèt per virulenta Danhaueri Scripta tùm temporis interversum, uti refert Autor p. 335.
latin.239: Post Cassellanum verò, Mavortis istius Germaniae, Libertatisque juxtà ac Religionis Statoris, optimô suô meritô, Autori nostro p. 341. dicti, FRIDERICI WILHELMI MAGNI Electoris Brandenburgici, pacifica conamina quam plurima, vel in vulgus nota sunt, similiter tamen à Theologis aliis, in vicinia Marchiae, Danhaueri istius vel Discipulis, vel Symmystis, pro exitiali, quô adversus Reformatos odio perciti erant, & Deum tantùm non blasphemè precabantur, quò se magis magisque odio Calvinianorum impleret, (nescientes profectò quid peterent,) praepedita.
latin.240: Quô pactô immortalis Gloriae Principi, Pietatis non minus in Deum & Sinceritatis Cordis sui, quàm Fortitudinis bellicae famâ, maximè inclyto, strenuo utrobique S. Davidis aemulatori, idem videtur accidisse, quod isti Hebraeo: Quemadmodum enim hic, maximo licèt Jehovae Templum aedificandi lapideum desiderio flagrans, ab instituto tamen, certis ex causis, prohibebatur, aedificandi negotio in filium Salomonem devolutô, cui etiam à Deo destinatum idem fuerat; ita simili prorsus modô Gloriosissimus Marchicorum Achilles, incredibili Pacis Evangelicae (à Suasore Autoreque Lipsiae olim quaesitae) indies magis magisque promovendae, zelo accensus, cum vel lacrymis, nobis, Differtatiunculam nostram de Pace Ecclesiastica, (speciali ejus jussu in vernaculam paulò post transferendam, Serenissimaeque ejus, tantô Heröe dignissimae Conjugi DOROTHEAE inscribendam) humillimè offerentibus testatus est, varia etiam de hac Pace, meditata sua tum temporis, uti aliàs pluries, aperturus clementissimè, pacisque studium perpetuum nobis, quantâ poterat vi virtuteque quâ pollebat maximâ, inculcaturus, Deo sic disponente, & ob causas soli sapientissimo notas, à Sacrario Pacis Protestanticae exstruendo abstractus est, supellectili tamen ad Sacrarium istud perficiendum, copiosiori à se collectâ, unà cum desiderio Pacis suo, in Filium suum, SALOMONEM NOSTRUM, undequaque pacificum, Regioque nunc Diademate à Deo exornatum, per haereditatem transmissâ.
latin.241: Hic REX NOSTER PIENTISSIMUS, ut aedificium Pacis Sacrae, (cujus Fundamentum praeteritô annô denuò jacere molitus est, exilique opellâ nostrâ, ad id quam clementissimè usus) benedicente Pacis DEO O. M. quàm felicissimè provehat, adque ipsum Fastigium, succurrentibus etiam aliis Regibus Principibusque, Almae Pacis Ecclesiasticae Promotoribus indefessis, in DEI Gloriam & Evangelicorum omnium Solatium Gaudiumque perducat, est, quod animitus vovemus precamurque. Rescriptum in hoc Negotio Regium, ad Episcopum suum primum, Reverendissimum Dominum BENJAMIN URSINUM, datum, & ex Germanico in Latinum versum, Lectori nostro hôc locô communicandum ducimus, quò de sincerissima AUGUSTI REGIS NOSTRI Intentione, deque Ejus studio, Pacem Ecclesiasticam promovendi fervidissimo, judicare cuivis integrum sit.

pass_a.236: §. VIII. Of either named Effort, the Leipzig and the Cassel, the fruit was not small, which extends itself not only to its own [age] in which they were undertaken and finished a few years ago, but even to the modern Century not so long begun.
pass_a.237: For besides that the better Theologians of either Party have grown accustomed thereafter to feel more mildly and kindly about themselves mutually and their Sects, and by their examples have led their hearers to do the same; so they have filled their Magistrates more and more with love and desire of reconciling Ecclesiastical Peace.
pass_a.238: For after the Leipzig Colloquy, Charles Louis the Palatine had a pacific Institute in hand, celebrated by our Author, although overturned at that time by Dannhauer’s virulent Writings, as the Author reports p. 335.
pass_a.239: But after the Cassel [colloquy], the very many pacific attempts of FREDERICK WILLIAM THE GREAT, Elector of Brandenburg — called by our Author p. 341, by his excellent desert, that Mars of Germany and Upholder of Liberty as well as Religion — are even known to the public, yet were likewise hindered by other Theologians in the neighborhood of the March, either Disciples or Symmystae of that Dannhauer, for the deadly hatred with which they were stirred against the Reformed, and they all but blasphemously prayed God that He would fill them more and more with hatred of the Calvinists (truly not knowing what they asked).
pass_a.240: By which means the same seems to have happened to the Prince of immortal Glory — most renowned no less for Piety toward God and Sincerity of his Heart than for fame of warlike Fortitude, a strenuous emulator of St. David on both sides — as happened to that Hebrew: For just as this one, though burning with greatest desire of building Jehovah a stone Temple, was yet prohibited from the undertaking for certain causes, the business of building having devolved upon his son Solomon, for whom the same had also been destined by God; so in an entirely similar way the Most Glorious Achilles of the Marchers, kindled with zeal of promoting day by day the incredible Evangelical Peace (once sought at Leipzig with him as Persuader and Author), when with even tears he testified to us humbly offering our little Dissertation on Ecclesiastical Peace (by his special command soon afterward to be transferred into the vernacular and inscribed to his Most Serene Consort DOROTHEA, most worthy of so great a Hero), and was about, as often elsewhere, most clemently to open his then meditations on this Peace and to inculcate perpetual zeal for peace upon us with all the force and virtue he possessed — God so disposing, and for causes known to the wisest Alone — he was drawn away from building the Sanctuary of Protestant Peace, yet with richer furniture collected by himself for finishing that Sanctuary, together with his desire of Peace, transmitted by inheritance to his Son, OUR SOLOMON, everywhere pacific and now adorned by God with the Royal Diadem.
pass_a.241: This OUR MOST PIOUS KING — that, with the blessing of the MOST HIGH GOD of Peace, he may advance as happily as possible the building of Sacred Peace (whose Foundation he strove again last year to lay, using our slight labor for it most clemently) and bring it to the very Summit, other Kings and Princes also helping as tireless Promoters of kindly Ecclesiastical Peace, unto the Glory of GOD and the Comfort and Joy of all Evangelicals — is what we vow and pray from the heart. The Royal Rescript in this Business, given to his first Bishop, the Most Reverend Lord BENJAMIN URSINUS, and turned from German into Latin, we judge should be communicated to our Reader in this place, so that it may be free for anyone to judge of the most sincere Intention of OUR AUGUST KING, and of His most fervent zeal for promoting Ecclesiastical Peace.

236: §. VIII. The fruit of both those Consociation attempts — Leipzig and Cassel — was not small.
It reaches not only the age in which they were begun and finished a few years back, but even our present century, itself not long under way.
237: For besides this: the better theologians on both sides grew used to thinking more mildly and kindly of one another and of their own parties, and by example led their hearers to do the same;
so they filled their magistrates more and more with love and desire for reconciling church peace.
238: After the Leipzig Colloquy, Charles Louis of the Palatinate had a pacific project in hand — one our Author celebrates —
though Dannhauer’s virulent writings then overturned it (Autor p. 335).
239: After Cassel, the many peace attempts of Frederick William the Great, Elector of Brandenburg — whom our Author (p. 341) rightly calls Germany’s Mars and upholder of liberty and religion — are even publicly known;
yet other theologians near the March, Dannhauer’s disciples or fellow-initiates, blocked them out of deadly hatred of the Reformed,
and all but blasphemously prayed God to fill them ever more with hatred of Calvinists — not knowing what they asked.
240: So the same seems to have befallen that prince of immortal glory — famed no less for piety toward God and sincerity of heart than for warlike fortitude, a strenuous emulator of St. David on both sides — as befell that Hebrew:
David burned to build Jehovah a stone temple, yet was barred from the work for set causes, and the building passed to his son Solomon, for whom God had also destined it;
likewise the most glorious Achilles of the Marchers, kindled with zeal to advance day by day the Evangelical peace once sought at Leipzig with him as persuader and author,

even with tears attested as much to us when we humbly offered our little Dissertation on Ecclesiastical Peace (which by his special order was soon to be put into the vernacular and dedicated to his most serene consort Dorothea, worthy of so great a hero),
and was about, as often before, most kindly to open his then thoughts on that peace and press perpetual peace-zeal upon us with all his force —
yet God so disposing, for reasons known to the All-wise alone, he was drawn off from raising the sanctuary of Protestant peace,

and transmitted by inheritance to his son — our Solomon, everywhere pacific, now crowned by God with the royal diadem — both richer furniture collected for finishing that sanctuary and his own desire for peace.
241: This is what we vow and pray from the heart for our Most Pious King:

that, with the Most High God of Peace blessing him, he may carry the building of Sacred Peace as happily as possible to its very summit — last year he again strove to lay its foundation, most kindly using our slight labor —
other kings and princes also helping as tireless promoters of kindly church peace, for God’s glory and the comfort and joy of all Evangelicals.
We judge the Royal Rescript in this business — given to his first bishop, the Most Reverend Lord Benjamin Ursinus, and turned from German into Latin — should be set before our reader here,
so anyone may judge the most sincere intention of our August King and his most fervent zeal to promote ecclesiastical peace.
Stop before the Rescript body (Nos Dei Gratia Fridericus Rex Borussiae…).
